title: What it means to run a real Rust compiler on an iPhone
summary: Follow a source file through local compilation, diagnostics, WASI execution, dependency preparation, and the practical limits of a phone-sized Rust workspace.

sections.heading: A compiler, not a remote text checker
paragraphs: The useful question is not whether an editor can color Rust syntax. It is whether a change to your program reaches a compiler that checks the same kinds of rules you would meet in a real project. Crabrix bundles a pinned Rust compiler and its wasm32-wasip1 sysroot inside the iOS app. When you press Check, that compiler parses your source, resolves names and types, and applies borrow checking on the device. The Problems view is fed by compiler diagnostics, not by a fixed set of quiz answers or a remote service pretending to understand the code.

That distinction changes how you learn. If you move a String into a function and use it again, the error comes from the language rules your own project must obey. If you misspell a variable, the highlighted span refers to your file. Fixing the program means changing the source and asking the compiler again. Crabrix still has to present the feedback clearly, but the verdict is produced by a real toolchain. The exact compiler target and toolchain identity are pinned for an app build so behavior can be compared and investigated rather than quietly changing from one session to the next.

sections.heading: From source to a result
paragraphs: There are four distinct stages in the usual loop. First, an editable source file lives in the project workspace. Second, the local compiler checks it and, for a requested build, produces a WASI binary. Third, Crabrix executes that binary in a fresh runtime store. Fourth, the program writes output or returns a result that the app shows in Output. The compiler can also report diagnostics along the way. A failed check stops before a new program can run; an empty Output panel after a successful build may simply mean the program never printed anything.

Keeping those stages separate helps with debugging. A red diagnostic is about code the compiler could not accept. A panic or nonzero exit after a successful build is about a program that did run. A line from println! belongs to stdout, not to the compiler. When you modify a file, predict which stage your change can affect before tapping Run. If a formatting placeholder is wrong, expect a compile-time message. If a branch prints only for one input, expect the build to succeed and output to vary with the input.

image.alt: Infographic showing source file, local Rust compiler, WASI binary, and local output inside an on-device boundary, with diagnostics branching from the compiler.
image.caption: The app keeps compilation and program execution as separate, observable steps.

sections.heading: What “local” does and does not promise
paragraphs: The compiler and runtime execute on the device. Source does not need to be uploaded to a compilation server for Check or Run. The app bundle contains the pinned compiler and sysroot; a phone does not download new compiler executable code to replace them. This is a concrete statement about the build loop, not a claim that every app feature is offline or that network access never occurs. Course downloads, a supported dependency that has not been cached, or importing a project can involve the network. A cached and pinned package archive can be reused for an offline rebuild under the conditions documented in the app.

A project terminal is likewise local but deliberately narrower than a Mac shell. It offers commands over the project workspace; it does not start arbitrary host processes or grant a Rust program unrestricted iOS access. The WASI guest has no network import. These limits protect the boundary between a user-edited project and the host app. They also matter when evaluating a crate: code that expects a native C library, an executable build script, or a socket opened by the guest cannot be assumed to work simply because it compiles on a desktop.

sections.heading: Why WebAssembly and WASI appear in the design
paragraphs: Rust normally compiles native code for a target platform. In Crabrix, the bundled compiler is itself a WebAssembly program run through CrabrixRuntime, a Swift interpreter derived from WasmKit. The project output targets wasm32-wasip1. That target gives a defined set of filesystem and process-style interfaces that the app can provide inside a bounded workspace. The runtime can meter execution, limit memory and output, and start a fresh store for program runs. This architecture is different from handing user source to a server or trying to execute an arbitrary new iOS binary.

The target is a compatibility choice, not a promise that every Rust ecosystem package will work. A pure Rust library that fits the supported target and build flow may be usable. A dependency that needs a host executable build.rs or a procedural macro requires capabilities outside the current local subset. The most honest workflow is to check a dependency before a long build, read the compatibility result, and keep an alternative design in mind. Often a small hand-written parser or a crate without native components is enough for a learning project.

sections.heading: The cost of genuine work
paragraphs: A real compiler performs genuine work, and a phone is not a desktop workstation. The first check of a changed project may spend time parsing, resolving packages, checking types, and generating code. Dependencies add more work. Repeating an identical build can benefit from local artifact caches, while changing source or configuration can invalidate some cached results. A spinner is not proof that the app is doing useful work by itself; a trustworthy interface should show which phase is active and surface errors when work stops.

For your own experiments, compare the right things. Run a tiny one-file program once, then run it again unchanged, then change one line and run again. Notice which run is fastest and which needs compilation. Avoid extrapolating from one warm cache measurement to a new Cargo project with dependencies. Limits on memory, writable files, runtime, and output can stop an overlarge guest. Treat those boundaries as part of the supported environment, just as a desktop toolchain has a target triple and system libraries that define its behavior.

sections.heading: Dependencies: useful, but selective
paragraphs: Cargo makes Rust projects larger than a single source file, and Crabrix supports a focused subset of that workflow. The app can resolve supported crates.io packages, verify downloaded archives against registry checksums, write a lockfile, and build suitable dependencies for its target. Once the exact verified source archives are cached or pinned for offline use, the same packages can be available without another download. That is a useful bridge from a tutorial snippet to a multi-file project with a manifest.

The subset has edges. Procedural-macro crates, executable build scripts, and native C linking are outside the supported local Cargo path. A package may depend on one of these indirectly, so read the whole dependency result rather than just the top-level crate name. A lockfile records a selected dependency graph, but it is not a magic guarantee that every dependency can be compiled for every target. Start with a small pure-Rust dependency, verify it works, then add one package at a time. That makes an incompatibility diagnosable instead of leaving you with a large unresolved graph.

sections.heading: A bounded workspace is a useful workspace
paragraphs: An editable project deserves to survive beyond the lesson that created it. Crabrix keeps project files in a local workspace, with a file tree, source editor, diagnostics, Output, and a project terminal. The terminal can help inspect files or run supported project commands, but it is not an unrestricted shell. That distinction is visible in the product because an honest tool should not imply that it can do what the platform and sandbox do not permit.

The runtime also protects itself from guest behavior. A program can loop forever, produce huge output, or request too much memory. Metering, deadlines, and output bounds give the app ways to stop or contain those cases. Stopping a guest is not the same as proving its algorithm correct; it is a resource policy that keeps the device responsive. When a build or run is interrupted, look at which phase stopped and whether a new binary was produced. Do not interpret an old Output line as the result of the latest failed build.

image.alt: A stylized phone code editor and diagnostics enclosed in a local sandbox.
image.caption: The project workspace is editable while the guest runtime stays inside explicit limits.

sections.heading: Read a diagnostic as evidence
paragraphs: Rust diagnostics often contain a primary message, a source span, notes, and sometimes a suggested change. Begin with the first meaningful error, not the last line in the panel. A missing brace can create many follow-up messages, so repair one cause and check again. If the compiler says “expected X, found Y,” identify which expression produced Y and which function or branch demanded X. This turns the error from a verdict into a map of the program you actually wrote.

For ownership errors, draw the flow of one value: creation, move, borrow, last use. A suggestion to clone may make code compile but can hide an unnecessary allocation or an unclear API. Ask whether a function needs ownership or only a read-only borrow. For a formatting error, count placeholders and supplied values. For a missing trait, inspect the operation that requires it. Each fix should be a conscious statement about the program, not a sequence of edits that happen to quiet the compiler.

sections.heading: A ten-minute experiment
paragraphs: Create a small project and write a function that returns a greeting. First compile and run the program unchanged, and record the exact output. Next misspell a binding name and press Check. Find the highlighted span, predict the smallest correction, then fix it. After that, add a second placeholder to println! but no second argument. Notice that this problem is caught before a new run. Finally restore a valid format and change the text the program prints. You have now observed source editing, compiler validation, a diagnostic, and runtime output as separate events.

Repeat the same method with a borrowed String: let a helper accept &str, call it with a String, and use the String afterward. Then change the helper to take ownership and compare the compiler response. This is more instructive than memorizing a slogan about borrowing. Keep a short note of each prediction, the actual evidence, and the rule you inferred. A local compiler is most valuable when it becomes a tool for testing your understanding, not just a button you press until the red text disappears.

sections.heading: Where to continue
paragraphs: The free Learn section on this website provides the same course topics and examples to read without an account. Start with Rust Basics if you are new to the language, then move through ownership and project structure before tackling concurrency or unsafe code. On the device, open an example in Code and make a durable project copy so you can experiment beyond the lesson. When a project grows, check the target and dependency limits before assuming desktop Cargo behavior.

Crabrix is a focused local Rust workspace. Its strength is that the edit, check, run, and inspect cycle can happen where you are, with a compiler whose identity and limits are visible. Its limits are part of that story. The fastest way to learn is to make a precise prediction, change one thing, read the evidence, and repeat.

title: From a Rust lesson to a project you own
summary: A practical path from reading one example to predicting behavior, editing source, handling errors, and keeping an independent Rust project.

sections.heading: Reading is a starting point
paragraphs: A short example can make a concept look obvious while someone else has already made every choice. You see a finished function, a correct type, and a successful output. The real skill starts when one detail changes: an input is empty, a value moves, or a branch returns the wrong type. Crabrix lessons are meant to give you an idea and a concrete Rust snippet, but the way to make that idea yours is to predict, edit, and check it. The compiler then tests a claim about your own code instead of asking you to remember someone else’s answer.

The Academy currently organizes six Rust courses with 142 guided lessons, plus Algorithm Atlas with 200 patterns across 600 steps. Those counts describe the catalog, not a promise that reading every page automatically makes someone fluent. A useful lesson has to make the next action clear: what to notice, what to change, what result to expect, and how to explain a surprise. On the website every lesson is open to read. In the app you can take an example into the editor and turn it into a project that remains yours.

sections.heading: The four-step learning loop
paragraphs: Begin by reading the example slowly enough to name each value and the operation that uses it. Before running anything, write down the output or the compiler error you expect. Then change one line and ask the same question again. Only after you have a prediction should you press Check or Run. Compare the evidence with your prediction, and revise your mental model if they differ. This order matters: without a prediction, even a surprising result is easy to accept without understanding.

For a tiny greeting, the prediction may be one exact line of stdout. For a borrow, predict whether the caller can still use the owned String after a function call. For a match, list every variant and which arm handles it. A failed prediction is useful when you can point to the rule you misunderstood. Keep the experiment small enough that one changed line has one plausible effect. If you change types, branches, and formatting all at once, the next diagnostic may tell you little about which idea was wrong.

image.alt: Infographic of the learning loop: read, predict, edit, check or run, and repeat.
image.caption: A prediction turns compiler feedback into an explanation you can test.

sections.heading: Copy the lesson into an independent project
paragraphs: In the iOS app, opening lesson source in Code creates an editable project copy. The project is separate from the downloaded course material. This is an important ownership boundary for the learner: you can make mistakes, rename files, or delete code without corrupting the lesson you may want to reread. You can also return to My Projects later rather than losing the experiment when you leave the lesson. The first copied version is only a starting point; the value lies in what you do to it.

Give the project a question. Instead of “I am practicing Rust,” try “What changes when this function borrows a String rather than taking it?” or “What should an empty list return?” Put that question in a note or comment, change the smallest relevant piece of code, and check. If the compiler rejects your experiment, read its message before undoing the change. If it succeeds, run an input that distinguishes your new behavior from the old one. A project becomes durable learning material when it records a sequence of understood decisions.

sections.heading: A concrete first experiment
paragraphs: Start with a list of names and a loop that prints a greeting for each one. Borrow the list during iteration so the list still exists afterward. Predict the output for two names, including punctuation and line breaks, then run it. Add a third name and predict again. This seems elementary, but it establishes the habit of separating collection contents, iteration, formatting, and output into distinct parts you can reason about.

Now remove the reference from the loop and try to use the list afterward. The compiler may tell you that the vector was moved by the iteration. Read the diagnostic as evidence about ownership: the loop took values rather than merely borrowing them. Restore the reference and explain why the later use works. Next try an empty vector. The loop runs zero times, so there is no greeting. Decide whether that is acceptable or whether your program should print an explicit “no names” message. You have moved from copying syntax to defining behavior for a boundary case.

sections.heading: Make compiler errors part of the plan
paragraphs: An error is most useful when you created it on purpose. Change `&names` to `names` in the loop, predict whether `names.len()` remains legal, and press Check. Identify the line where ownership moved and the later line that tried to use the old binding. Do not immediately add `.clone()` merely to remove the error. Cloning can be correct when independent owned copies are needed, but in this example a borrow expresses the intent more clearly and avoids copying elements.

Try a different controlled mistake: give a function an `i32` argument where it expects `&str`. The diagnostic compares the actual and expected types. Ask whether the caller should convert its value, or whether the function signature is wrong for your intended API. That question is more valuable than a mechanical cast. Fix one error, compile again, and only then inspect the next. Compiler messages often cascade from one missing delimiter or type mismatch, so treating every line as an independent bug wastes time.

sections.heading: Handle the first real input
paragraphs: A copied example often contains only known-good values. A real project eventually reads text it did not choose. Parsing is the first useful boundary to add. Accept a text number, call `parse::<i32>()`, and handle both `Ok(number)` and `Err(error)`. Decide what the user should see when the input is empty, contains letters, or exceeds the number type’s range. This is where a tutorial becomes software: you must define behavior for the cases the original snippet did not show.

Keep the failure path recoverable. An `unwrap()` may be fine in a five-line controlled demonstration, but it turns ordinary bad input into a panic. Returning `Result` from a helper lets its caller decide whether to retry, show a message, or stop. Add a test or a small table of inputs and expected outcomes. If you cannot explain why a failed parse is handled one way rather than another, the project needs a clearer requirement. The compiler ensures you handle the type; the product decision is still yours.

sections.heading: Grow the file tree deliberately
paragraphs: One file is enough for a first experiment. Split code into modules when a boundary is clear, not merely because the file reached a certain line count. A parser module can own conversion and error messages; a model module can define the values the rest of the project uses; main can connect input to output. If a function is useful from another module, decide whether to expose it with `pub`. Keep internal helpers private. This gives names to responsibilities while keeping the public API small.

The project workspace supports multiple files and a manifest. Some projects can add supported crates.io dependencies, but check target compatibility before building a design around one. A dependency may transitively require a build script, procedural macro, or native linker that the local target does not support. Start with a small pure-Rust dependency and verify it before adding more. The moment you add files or packages, keep a working version of the project so you can distinguish a module-path error from a dependency problem.

image.alt: An illustrated lesson page becoming a separate project folder with editable source files.
image.caption: The lesson stays a reference; the editable project becomes the place for your experiments.

sections.heading: Use tests for claims you want to keep
paragraphs: A print statement answers “what happened in this run?” A test can preserve a claim for future changes. For a greeting function, test a normal name and an empty name. For parsing, test valid, invalid, and boundary inputs. Name the test after the behavior it protects rather than the method it calls. A test that merely repeats implementation details can pass even while the user-facing result is wrong. Keep expected values visible and specific.

Choose the smallest useful test. A pure function can be tested without invoking the entire app. An integration-style test can check that several modules work together. A manual run is still useful for terminal output and interaction, but it should not be the only guard for a rule you plan to rely on. After changing a function, run the relevant tests and then check the project again. If a test fails, decide whether the behavior or the expectation should change; do not update expected output automatically without understanding the difference.

sections.heading: Debug with a hypothesis
paragraphs: When a program produces the wrong answer, start with one hypothesis that could explain it. “The empty input takes the normal branch” is testable; “Rust is behaving strangely” is not. Inspect the value just before the branch, or add a narrow temporary debug print. Compare it with the value you predicted. If the hypothesis fails, remove that observation and choose another. This is faster than scattering prints across every line and trying to read an ocean of logs afterward.

Separate build errors from runtime behavior. Problems contains compiler diagnostics from code that could not be accepted. Output is where a built program’s stdout and run outcome appear. The project terminal offers supported commands over the workspace, not an unrestricted host shell. Use the tool that answers your current question. If a run was interrupted, confirm whether the visible output belongs to the latest build or an earlier one. Write a regression test after you understand the bug so the same boundary stays covered.

sections.heading: Keep the result and choose the next question
paragraphs: A project copy is useful because it remains editable after the lesson ends. Rename it to describe the experiment, keep the source and tests that explain its behavior, and export it when you want to move it elsewhere. A downloaded course can be updated independently of that project. Offline reading and offline building also differ: a course can be stored on the phone while an exercise using an uncached dependency may still require preparation. Plan accordingly before a trip or a class without connectivity.

One good learning session is not measured by the number of lessons completed. It is measured by a rule you can now explain and a program whose behavior you can predict. After Rust Basics, try ownership with a deliberate move and borrow; after that, build a small multi-file program with one recoverable error. Return to the free web lesson when you need the reference, then use the local compiler to test the next claim. Over time, your project collection becomes evidence of what you can actually make.

title: Rust dependency graphs: deterministic plans and honest cycle errors
summary: Implement a deterministic topological planner in Rust, reject missing dependencies, and report a real cycle witness without blaming every blocked package.

sections.heading: A build order should explain why each step is ready
paragraphs: A compiler, a static-site generator and a data pipeline all need to answer a similar question: which work can begin after its prerequisites have completed? A list of names is insufficient once one operation depends on another. You need a graph, a clear edge direction, a readiness rule and an error that distinguishes a missing prerequisite from a cycle. Otherwise a stalled pipeline tends to report whichever task happened to be inspected last.

This tutorial builds a deterministic planner using Rust's standard ordered collections. It returns prerequisites before consumers, rejects references to unknown nodes and reports one actual cycle when no complete order exists. It also reports every node blocked by unresolved cyclic work without claiming that every blocked node is itself part of a cycle. That distinction is useful in package managers, lesson prerequisites, document generation and background jobs whose dependencies need to be explained to a user.

image.alt: Ivory task blocks on a navy engineering board form a jade branching dependency graph beside a separate coral triangular cycle.
image.caption: A useful plan describes dependency readiness and distinguishes an actual cycle from the work waiting behind it.

sections.heading: Define edge direction in words before drawing arrows
paragraphs: Our input maps each package to the packages it requires. If `web` contains `core` in its dependency set, web depends on core and core must appear earlier in the successful order. When the planner constructs its reverse index, it records web as a consumer of core. These are two views of the same relationship, and confusing them reverses the resulting build order while still producing output that may look superficially plausible.

Use a tiny chain as the first fixture: config has no dependencies, core depends on config, and web depends on core. The only valid order is config, core, web. That fixture catches a reversed interpretation immediately. In documentation and diagrams, label arrows with the relationship they express. An arrow meaning depends on points in the opposite direction from one meaning enables, so an unlabeled diagram can undermine an otherwise correct implementation.

sections.heading: Treat missing nodes as a different input error
paragraphs: A referenced dependency that is absent from the graph is not automatically a leaf. Perhaps the caller forgot to resolve it, filtered it out incorrectly or misspelled its name. Pretending it is ready would produce a plan with a missing prerequisite. The example validates every dependency before scheduling any work and returns both the package and the unknown dependency in its error.

This validation boundary is intentionally separate from downloading or resolving packages. A resolver decides which exact package instance a requirement names; the planner receives an already identified graph. Combining those responsibilities can make a registry failure look like a graph cycle or make a dependency-version conflict disappear into an empty node. Keep the stages separate enough that an error can name the decision that failed and the information needed to reproduce it.

sections.heading: Make duplicate edges an explicit normalization choice
paragraphs: The graph stores dependencies in a `BTreeSet`, so listing the same dependency twice creates one edge. Readiness counts are computed from that normalized set. This matters because decrementing a prerequisite count once per consumer relationship only works when the count and the reverse index represent the same edges. Counting duplicate declarations while storing unique consumers can leave a node permanently blocked even though every real prerequisite completed.

Normalization is a domain decision, not a universal rule. Two build steps may require distinct outputs from the same package, in which case those output requirements should be modeled explicitly rather than collapsed accidentally. Our nodes represent complete tasks and each dependency relationship means that one complete prerequisite task must finish. Repeated declarations of that exact relationship are redundant, which is why set semantics match the example's contract.

sections.heading: Choose a deterministic ready queue
paragraphs: Several tasks may be ready at the same time. Any order among independent ready tasks can be topologically valid, but choosing an order reproducibly makes logs, snapshots and bug reports easier to compare. The planner uses a `BTreeSet` and removes its first element, so it consistently chooses the lexicographically smallest currently ready name. Input insertion order does not decide which task is selected next.

That tie-break rule does not imply that alphabetical order is the best production scheduler. A real scheduler might prioritize the critical path, user-visible work, memory limits or cache hits. Determinism is the requirement here, and lexical ordering is a small policy that is easy to test. If you later change the policy, keep topological correctness separate from the tie-break rule so a performance change does not accidentally weaken prerequisite enforcement.

sources.title: Rust standard library: ordered BTreeSet operations

sections.heading: Follow one successful plan step by step
paragraphs: Each package begins with a count of unfinished prerequisites. The initial ready set contains packages whose count is zero. Taking a ready package appends it to the output order and decrements the counts of its consumers. A consumer enters the ready set exactly when its count reaches zero. No scan of the entire graph is needed after every completion because the reverse consumer index identifies the affected nodes.

In the runnable fixture, config enables core, then core enables both cli and web. The ordered ready set chooses cli before web. Neither consumer is allowed to run before core, and both remain valid independent choices afterward. This trace is small enough to write on paper, which makes it a useful debugging tool when a larger graph appears to schedule work prematurely or never releases a package that should be ready.

image.alt: A dependency readiness trace shows config enabling core and core enabling cli and web; a separate cycle a-b blocks c without placing c in the cycle.
image.caption: Arrows in the readiness example mean enables. The cycle witness uses depends-on edges and names only the nodes on the closed walk.

sections.heading: Run the complete deterministic planner
paragraphs: Save this program as `main.rs` and run it with edition 2021. It needs no downloaded packages. The main function checks a successful branching graph and a graph with a two-node cycle plus a downstream consumer. Compiling the same file as a test harness checks an unknown prerequisite, an empty graph and repeated declarations of the same edge. The code returns structured errors rather than constructing a user-facing sentence inside the algorithm.

The example uses short string names for readability. A real package planner should use an identity that distinguishes versions, sources, targets and other build-unit properties relevant to that system. Two packages with the same display name are not necessarily the same node. Resolving that identity before planning prevents a successful topological order from concealing an incorrectly merged dependency graph.

sections.heading: Understand what Kahn’s algorithm leaves behind
paragraphs: If the output contains every node, the plan is complete. Otherwise the ready set became empty while some nodes still had unfinished prerequisites. Those remaining nodes are blocked by the unresolved subgraph. At least one cycle exists in that subgraph, but other remaining nodes may merely depend on a cycle. Reporting the entire remaining set as the cycle would therefore accuse nodes that cannot fix the underlying problem.

Our error includes both `blocked` and `witness`. The blocked list tells the caller which work could not be scheduled. The witness identifies one closed dependency walk that can explain a real cycle. A user interface can show the witness prominently and list downstream affected packages separately. That gives a developer a smaller relationship to inspect while preserving the broader impact of the failure.

sections.heading: Find a cycle witness without recursive traversal
paragraphs: After the ready queue is exhausted, every blocked node has at least one dependency that is also blocked. If it did not, all its prerequisites would already have completed and it would have become ready. The witness search starts at the first blocked node and repeatedly follows one blocked dependency. Because the remaining graph is finite, the walk must eventually revisit a node. The repeated suffix is a closed dependency walk.

The `positions` map remembers where each visited node first appeared in the walk. When a repeated node is found, slicing from its previous position and appending that node closes the witness. Prefix nodes are excluded: they may lead into a cycle without belonging to it. This iterative approach also avoids consuming the Rust call stack in a deeply nested graph. It finds one witness, not a complete decomposition into all strongly connected components.

sections.heading: Do not confuse a cycle witness with every cycle
paragraphs: A graph can contain several independent cycles or one larger strongly connected region with many possible closed walks. The example reports one deterministic witness, which is enough to establish that a complete topological order is impossible. Fixing that relationship may reveal another cycle on the next run. If your product needs to display every cyclic region at once, use a strongly connected component analysis and distinguish each region from its downstream consumers.

For a package installer, one witness may be sufficient for an actionable first error. For a visual dependency editor, showing all cyclic groups can be more helpful because users may repair several relationships in one interaction. Decide based on the workflow, and name the result accurately. A field called all_cycles would be misleading for this implementation, whereas witness communicates both what the algorithm found and the limit of that evidence.

sections.heading: A plan is not yet a parallel scheduler
paragraphs: The returned vector is a valid serial order. It does not create worker threads, enforce resource quotas or decide when a failed task should cancel its consumers. Parallel execution needs to preserve the same readiness invariant while tracking tasks that are queued, running, completed or failed. Decrement a consumer's unfinished count after a prerequisite succeeds, not merely after it starts or enters a worker queue.

Keep scheduling policy and execution state out of the immutable input graph when possible. The graph explains the dependency relationships; an operation-specific state structure records this run's progress. That separation helps when a user cancels a build, retries one package or compares a cached run with a fresh one. Reusing a graph must not accidentally reuse a previous run's half-decremented counters or stale running flags.

sections.heading: Cache evidence belongs to the exact build unit
paragraphs: A planner can treat a verified cached prerequisite as already satisfied, but only after establishing that the artifact matches the requested build unit. A package name alone is not enough. Source content, selected features, dependency identities, compiler inputs and target configuration can all change what a package produces. Cache reuse therefore needs a separate validity decision before it influences scheduling.

In a learning application, keep the visible labels honest. A package loaded from a valid artifact cache should appear as cached, while a newly compiled package should appear as compiled. A metadata-only check should not be presented as a successful executable run. Those distinctions are useful when investigating a reported boundary: the graph may be correct and the cache entry valid for Check, while linking or execution still exposes a missing backend operation.

sections.heading: Progress counts need a clear denominator
paragraphs: A dependency graph gives a useful count of planned work, but package count is not elapsed-time prediction. Ten tiny libraries may compile faster than one large generic library. If a user sees nine of ten packages completed, the final package can still dominate the run. Show the count as completed units alongside the current package and stage, rather than implying that ninety percent of the total time has passed.

The denominator can also change if resolution is still discovering the graph. Avoid reporting a final total before the relevant planning stage has completed. A good event stream can say resolving dependencies first, then publish the known package list, then report acquisition, verification and compilation transitions. This makes a stalled source download distinguishable from a slow compiler invocation without introducing a decorative percentage that obscures the actual operation.

sections.heading: Reject duplicate node declarations during ingestion
paragraphs: The graph type has unique keys by construction, but that does not mean every input format is already unambiguous. Collecting repeated node declarations into a map can replace an earlier declaration with a later one. If the two declarations disagree about prerequisites, the resulting graph may be valid while no longer representing what the source actually said. Detect that conflict before constructing the planner's normalized input.

The small `graph` helper in the program constructs test fixtures; its rows are deliberately unique. A parser for a real manifest or job file should return a duplicate-node error with the relevant source locations. Identical repeated declarations may be rejected or merged under a documented rule, but contradictory declarations should not be resolved by whichever entry happened to arrive last.

This is another reason to separate parsing, normalization and planning. A missing field, duplicate identity and structural cycle need different repairs. Once the planner receives a validated map of unique identities and normalized dependency sets, its readiness counts can describe that graph precisely rather than compensating for ambiguities it no longer has enough source information to explain.

sections.heading: A failed prerequisite is not a newly discovered cycle
paragraphs: Suppose a valid acyclic plan begins executing and core fails to compile. Its consumers cannot proceed, but that runtime state has not introduced a cycle into the dependency graph. If an execution controller simply leaves their unfinished counts nonzero and runs the cycle-reporting branch, it can produce an impossible diagnosis. Structural planning and runtime success tracking must remain distinct.

Give the execution layer explicit states such as waiting, running, succeeded, failed and blocked by failed prerequisite. When core fails, its own diagnostic explains the cause, while downstream tasks can name core as the reason they did not run. Keep those tasks visible if a user wants to understand the impact, but avoid repeating the entire compiler error under every dependent package.

A retry can then reset the affected execution states without changing the graph. After the prerequisite succeeds, consumers become eligible under the original readiness rules. Testing this transition is particularly useful for an interactive compiler, where a user commonly fixes one dependency or project file and expects the same open project to continue through the previously blocked stages.

sections.heading: Build units may need identities finer than package names
paragraphs: One package can participate in several distinct build units. Host-side build tools and target-side libraries may need different feature sets or compilation settings, even when they come from the same source version. An alias can also give a dependency a different name in a consumer's source. Neither an alias nor a bare registry name is a complete universal build identity.

For a real compiler integration, resolve those distinctions before feeding nodes to a topological planner. Include the source and exact version, target role and relevant configuration in the unit identity; retain aliases on the edges where consumers use them. Do not unify a build script's dependencies with a target library's dependencies merely to make the graph easier to represent. A deterministic order over incorrectly merged nodes is still an incorrect build.

The tutorial's strings keep the algorithm readable, but the algorithm itself does not require display names as keys. Replacing them with an ordered domain-specific identifier should preserve readiness and cycle semantics while allowing the presentation layer to show a shorter friendly label.

sections.heading: Test the returned order as a property
paragraphs: For every successful plan, build a map from node name to output position and assert that every prerequisite appears before its consumer. Also assert that the output contains every graph node exactly once. These properties catch missing nodes and premature scheduling even when a test does not require a particular tie-break policy. A separate test can require the lexical order chosen by this implementation.

For a cycle error, verify every adjacent pair in the witness against the original depends-on relation and verify that the first and last nodes are equal. Check that every witness node appears in blocked, but do not require every blocked node to appear in the witness. A deliberately downstream node such as c in the example makes that distinction observable. Tests should protect the meaning of an error field, not just compare a convenient formatted string.

sections.heading: Keep import and resolution failures at their own boundary
paragraphs: A real repository can fail before this planner receives a graph. Its workspace may require a selected member, a dependency may come from an unavailable Git revision, or an optional feature may introduce a native toolchain. These are not graph-cycle failures merely because dependency preparation stopped. Preserve the original failure category and enough context to identify the unresolved requirement.

Likewise, a successful plan establishes order, not target compatibility. A library can be correctly ordered and still fail because its code uses a missing operating-system API or exposes a compiler backend defect. A useful build report keeps source acquisition, graph resolution, planning, compilation and execution as distinct stages. That separation makes it possible to improve the missing capability and rerun exactly the stage that failed without rewriting an otherwise correct explanation of the dependency graph.

sections.heading: Use the graph to make failures smaller and clearer
paragraphs: The planner's main contribution is an explanation that survives changes in input order and execution timing. A successful result says which prerequisites make each step possible. A missing-node error names the incomplete relationship. A cycle result supplies one real closed walk and a separate list of affected work. Those outputs are small enough to log, compare in tests and show in an interface without exposing the entire internal implementation.

When extending the algorithm, keep those meanings intact. Add domain-specific identities before planning, choose a tie-break rule deliberately, validate cached prerequisites separately and model execution progress outside the immutable graph. Whether the application builds Rust libraries, renders a set of web pages or schedules learning exercises, the useful invariant remains concrete: a task becomes ready because every required predecessor has successfully supplied what it needs.

title: Rust generational handles: keep identity when storage is reused
summary: Implement a safe Rust arena with owner identities, reusable slots and checked generations. Reject stale handles, test removal boundaries and plan persistence carefully.

sections.heading: The wrong object can be a completely memory-safe result
paragraphs: A project list stores documents in a vector. An asynchronous operation remembers that the selected document is at index three. The user closes that document, another document takes its place, and the operation eventually reports a result for index three. Every array access can be within bounds and every reference can obey Rust's borrow rules, yet the visible result belongs to the wrong document. Memory safety has not been violated; application identity has.

A generational handle separates the reusable position from the lifetime of its occupant. This article builds a small arena that stores values in slots, reuses empty slots and rejects handles from earlier occupants. It also gives each arena an owner identity, because a slot and generation alone cannot distinguish two independent collections. The implementation uses ordinary safe Rust and the standard library. Its purpose is to make the invariants understandable before choosing a mature arena library for a larger system.

image.alt: An old coral identification tag lies apart from a brass specimen rack where an ivory tray now contains a new jade specimen.
image.caption: A reused position is not the same object. A handle needs enough identity to tell those cases apart.

sections.heading: Start by stating what an identifier promises
paragraphs: An index promises a position in a collection under some set of mutation rules. A stable object identifier promises that a later lookup either finds the same logical object or reports that it no longer exists. Those are different promises. If your collection only appends and never removes, an index may satisfy your application's needs. If removal, compaction or asynchronous callbacks are involved, write down the mutation rules before deciding that an index is enough.

A handle in our arena contains an arena identity, a slot index and a generation. Lookup checks all three relevant conditions: the handle belongs to this arena, the index exists, and the slot still has the same generation and a live value. A missing object becomes `None`, which the caller can handle deliberately. There is no fallback to the new occupant, and the lookup never tries to reconstruct an object from a remembered address.

sections.heading: Why vector movement is not the only problem
paragraphs: A vector may reallocate its storage when it grows. Rust's borrowing rules prevent safe code from retaining an ordinary borrowed element reference across a conflicting mutation that could invalidate it. A copied integer index has no such lifetime relationship. It remains a perfectly valid integer after the collection changes, even when its old meaning has disappeared. Solving relocation alone therefore does not solve the stale-identity problem.

Removal policies introduce further choices. Ordered removal shifts later elements, while swapping an element with the last position changes which object occupies a particular index. A slot-based arena avoids moving occupied logical positions during removal, but an empty position may later be reused. The generation is what distinguishes reuse from continuity. Think of these as separate decisions about memory location, ordering and object lifetime rather than treating every collection mutation as the same kind of instability.
